title: The Dead Woman
excerpt: A missing woman appears in an old news photograph—and she looks exactly like Maya.
content:
*Day Three — 12:01 a.m.*

The little girl in the photograph had Maya's eyes.

That was the first thing she noticed.

The second was the blood.

It stained the front of the child's white dress, spreading from her waist to the hem. Her small fingers wrapped around the handle of a kitchen knife, and her face was turned toward the camera with an expression that was neither frightened nor confused.

She looked calm.

That frightened Maya more than the blood.

She sat on the floor of Meridian House, staring at the photograph while Daniel leaned against the hospital bed, trying to steady his breathing.

“Tell me that's not me,” she whispered.

Daniel didn't answer.

“Tell me!”

He reached for the photograph, but she pulled it away.

“I've never held a knife like that. I've never hurt anybody.”

“Maya, we don't know when this photograph was taken.”

“That's my face.”

“I know.”

“Then why aren't you saying anything?”

“Because I'm trying to understand what we're looking at.”

She stood abruptly and began pacing the room.

Dr. Shaw had disappeared. The door to the corridor remained open, and somewhere deeper inside the abandoned facility, a mechanical alarm sounded at regular intervals.

Maya wanted to run.

She wanted to go home, lock every door, and pretend the past eleven years had never happened.

But she knew she couldn't.

Not anymore.

She turned back to Daniel.

“Who is Rebecca?”

He looked exhausted.

“My sister was twenty-three when she started working at Meridian House. She had studied medical administration and wanted to become a hospital manager. She believed the foundation was doing good work.”

“What did she discover?”

“Records that didn't match the patients. People were being admitted under false names. Some were discharged without any documentation. Others disappeared entirely.”

“Were they conducting experiments?”

“That's what Rebecca suspected.”

Daniel rubbed his face.

“She told me she had found a patient whose records described procedures that weren't approved by the hospital. She wanted to report it. A week later, she disappeared.”

Maya looked down at the photograph.

“And you think I was involved?”

“I think somebody wants you to believe you were.”

“Why?”

“Because if you believe you killed Rebecca, you'll stop looking for the person who actually made her disappear.”

Maya considered that.

It made sense.

But the photograph remained in her hand.

The child's face was unmistakable.

“What if I did something?” she whispered. “What if they made me forget?”

Daniel stood.

“Then we'll find out what happened. But we won't let Shaw decide what the truth is.”

Maya nodded slowly.

They left Meridian House through a service entrance and drove to Daniel's apartment. He insisted that they avoid her building because the unknown men might still be watching it.

His apartment was small and untidy, with books stacked on the dining table and unopened mail covering the kitchen counter. A photograph of Daniel and Rebecca stood beside the television.

Maya stopped when she saw it.

Rebecca was smiling.

She had dark hair, warm brown eyes, and a small scar across her chin.

The same scar as the woman in Maya's childhood photograph.

“Did she ever mention my family?” Maya asked.

Daniel looked at the photograph.

“Once.”

“When?”

“Two weeks before she disappeared.”

“What did she say?”

He hesitated.

“She said there was a little girl at Meridian House who reminded her of herself.”

Maya's throat tightened.

“What else?”

“She said the girl was frightened of the doctors. She wanted to help her.”

Maya looked at the photograph again.

“Was I that girl?”

“I don't know.”

“You must have some idea.”

Daniel sat down.

“Rebecca told me she had found a way to get one patient out of the facility. She said the girl's mother had agreed to help. But the night they planned to leave, something went wrong.”

“What happened?”

“She never told me.”

Maya stared at him.

“Why didn't you tell me any of this before?”

“Because I didn't know the little girl was you.”

He took the photograph from her and examined the back.

There was a series of numbers written beneath the date.

014 — 22:40 — ROOM 7.

Daniel opened his laptop.

“I know someone who might be able to identify this.”

“Who?”

“A former nurse who worked at Meridian House. She left the facility shortly before the fire.”

“Do you trust her?”

“No.”

Maya raised an eyebrow.

“That's reassuring.”

“I trust that she's afraid of whoever ran that place. Sometimes fear makes people tell the truth.”

He searched his contacts and found a number.

After several attempts, someone answered.

A woman's voice whispered, “I told you never to call me again.”

“It's Daniel Okafor.”

Silence.

Then the woman said, “I know who you are.”

“I need to ask you about a patient.”

“No.”

“Please. It's important.”

“I said no.”

“The patient's name was Maya Cole.”

The silence that followed felt endless.

Finally, the woman spoke.

“Where did you get that name?”

“We found a photograph.”

“Destroy it.”

Maya moved closer to the phone.

“Why?”

The woman began speaking quickly.

“You shouldn't be asking these questions. You shouldn't even know about that facility. They told me you had died.”

Maya's heart began to race.

“Who told you that?”

“Your father.”

The call ended.

Daniel immediately called back.

The number was switched off.

Maya stared at him.

“Find her.”

“I'm trying.”

“No. Find her.”

Daniel reopened his laptop and searched the number through old records. After several minutes, he found an address linked to the former nurse.

Her name was Grace Adebayo.

She lived in a small town outside Lagos, in a house registered to a relative.

Maya grabbed her bag.

“Let's go.”

Daniel looked at the clock.

“It's almost two in the morning.”

“I don't care.”

“Maya, we should wait until daylight.”

She turned toward him.

“Every day, somebody tells me to wait. My father waited. My mother waited. You waited. And now people are dying while I stand around trying to decide whether I'm allowed to know the truth.”

She walked toward the door.

“I'm done waiting.”

Daniel followed her.

Neither of them noticed the small camera hidden above the television.

Its red indicator blinked once.

Then a message appeared on a screen in a room hundreds of kilometres away.

SUBJECT 014 HAS LEFT THE FACILITY.

A reply arrived seconds later.

LET HER GO TO GRACE.

Another message followed.

SHE WILL REMEMBER EVERYTHING THERE.

---

## The Nurse's Confession

At 7:18 a.m., Maya and Daniel arrived at Grace Adebayo's house.

The building stood at the end of a narrow road, surrounded by a rusted fence and overgrown shrubs. The curtains were drawn, and a handwritten sign on the gate warned visitors not to enter without permission.

Daniel knocked.

No answer.

He knocked again.

A voice came from inside.

“Go away.”

“Grace, it's Daniel. We spoke on the phone.”

“I'm calling the police.”

“Please, just five minutes.”

A lock clicked.

The gate opened a few inches.

An elderly woman stared at them through the gap. Her hair was almost entirely grey, and deep lines crossed her forehead.

When she saw Maya, she stepped backward.

“Oh, my God.”

Maya swallowed.

“Please tell me what happened.”

Grace looked down the road.

Then she opened the gate.

“Come inside.”

The house smelled of antiseptic and old books. Photographs covered the walls, most of them showing children in school uniforms or families gathered around birthday cakes.

Grace led them into a small sitting room and locked the door.

“You look like your mother,” she told Maya.

“Everyone keeps saying that.”

“Because it's true.”

Grace sat down and folded her hands.

“I thought you'd died.”

“Why?”

“Because that's what Dr. Shaw told us.”

Maya leaned forward.

“When?”

“The night of the fire.”

Grace closed her eyes.

“I worked at Meridian House for almost six years. Officially, I was a nurse in the research department. Unofficially, I was responsible for patients who couldn't be explained to their families.”

“What does that mean?”

“Some were children whose parents had signed consent forms they didn't understand. Others were adults who had agreed to treatment without being told what the treatment involved.”

Maya felt sick.

“And me?”

Grace looked at her.

“You were different.”

“How?”

“You weren't admitted because you were ill.”

Maya gripped the edge of her chair.

“Then why was I there?”

Grace took a long breath.

“Your father brought you to Meridian House after an incident at home. You had experienced something traumatic, and he was convinced that if you remembered it, you would be in danger.”

“What incident?”

“I don't know the whole story. I was told you had witnessed something you shouldn't have.”

Maya looked at Daniel.

He was watching Grace intently.

“What happened to my memories?” Maya asked.

Grace hesitated.

“The doctors were experimenting with methods of influencing memory recall. They used medication, repeated questioning, controlled environments, and other techniques. They believed they could make certain traumatic memories less accessible.”

“Could they make someone forget an entire person?”

“Not reliably. Memory is complicated. But they could influence what a patient recalled, how confident they felt about a memory, and whether certain reminders triggered distress.”

“So they made me forget Rebecca?”

“I don't know.”

Maya stood.

“Everyone says that. Nobody knows anything.”

Grace reached for her wrist.

“I know one thing.”

Maya stopped.

“On the night of the fire, you were supposed to leave with your mother. Rebecca was helping her. Your father had arranged for a car to take you both away.”

“What went wrong?”

“Dr. Shaw discovered the plan.”

Grace's voice trembled.

“He locked down the research wing. Your mother managed to get you out, but Rebecca went back inside to retrieve something.”

“What?”

“A recording.”

Grace walked to a cupboard and removed a small metal box.

Inside was an old cassette tape, a photograph, and a folded sheet of paper.

She handed Maya the photograph first.

It showed Rebecca standing beside a hospital bed.

A child lay beneath a white blanket.

The child's face was obscured.

On the back was a handwritten note.

IF ANYTHING HAPPENS TO ME, THE TRUTH IS IN THE ORIGINAL RECORDING.

Maya picked up the cassette.

“What is this?”

“Rebecca gave it to me the week before she disappeared. She said it contained evidence of what was happening at Meridian House.”

“Why didn't you give it to the police?”

“Because I was told Rebecca was dead.”

“By whom?”

Grace looked at Maya.

“Your father.”

The room fell silent.

Maya sat down again.

For the first time, she began to wonder whether her father's secrecy had been motivated by something more complicated than shame.

Perhaps he had been trying to save her.

Perhaps he had been involved in the very operation he wanted her to escape.

Perhaps he had done both.

“Can we play the tape?” Daniel asked.

Grace shook her head.

“Not here.”

“Why?”

“Because this house isn't safe.”

She walked to the window and carefully moved the curtain.

A black vehicle stood across the road.

Its engine was running.

Maya felt her stomach tighten.

“Is that them?”

Grace didn't answer.

Instead, she opened a door leading to the kitchen.

“There is a back exit. You should leave now.”

Maya took the cassette and put it in her bag.

“What about you?”

“I'll be fine.”

“Grace—”

“Listen to me. If you want to know what happened to Rebecca, find the original research archive. Not the files your father kept. Not the copies Daniel found.”

She pressed a folded piece of paper into Maya's hand.

“The original archive is beneath the old chapel at Meridian House.”

Maya stared at her.

“There's a chapel?”

“There was. They converted it into a storage room before the fire.”

A car door slammed outside.

Grace flinched.

“Go!”

Daniel pulled Maya toward the back door.

As they hurried through the kitchen, Grace called after them.

“One more thing!”

Maya turned.

Grace's face had gone pale.

“Whatever you remember about Rebecca, don't assume you remember it correctly.”

Then the front door burst open.

A man's voice shouted from the sitting room.

“Grace Adebayo! Don't move!”

Daniel pushed Maya through the back exit.

They ran into the narrow alley behind the house and didn't stop until they reached the main road.

When they finally reached the car, Maya looked at the folded paper.

It contained a set of coordinates and a handwritten sentence.

THE DEAD WOMAN IS NOT THE ONE YOU THINK.

---

## The Photograph

They drove to a small hotel where Daniel had booked a room under a false name.

Maya sat on the edge of the bed while Daniel checked the doors and windows.

The cassette lay on the bedside table.

She couldn't stop thinking about Grace's warning.

Don't assume you remember it correctly.

“What if Rebecca is alive?” Maya asked.

Daniel turned.

“Then I'll find her.”

“What if she's the person sending the messages?”

He stared at her.

“Why would she want to kill you?”

“I don't know. Maybe she thinks I killed her.”

“You were a child.”

“Maybe that doesn't matter to her.”

Daniel sat beside her.

“Maya, listen to me. Whatever happened at Meridian House, we need evidence. We can't let fear fill in the gaps.”

She nodded, but she wasn't convinced.

They found an old cassette player in the hotel's reception office. Daniel persuaded the manager to lend it to them, claiming it contained an important family recording.

Back in the room, Maya inserted the tape.

A hiss filled the speakers.

Then a woman's voice emerged.

Rebecca.

“My name is Rebecca Okafor. If anyone finds this recording, it means I wasn't able to get the evidence out of Meridian House.”

There was a pause.

“I have spent three years working in the research department. At first, I believed we were helping patients recover from trauma. Then I discovered that some of the records were being altered.”

The recording continued.

“Patients were given numbers instead of names. Their memories were tested repeatedly. Some were subjected to procedures they hadn't consented to. When they complained, their records were changed to make them appear unstable.”

Maya covered her mouth.

Rebecca's voice became quieter.

“There is one child in particular. Subject 014. Her father brought her here after an incident involving a woman named Evelyn Cole.”

Maya froze.

Her mother.

Rebecca continued.

“The child has been told that her mother abandoned her. That isn't true. Evelyn has been trying to get her daughter out of this facility for months.”

Daniel looked at Maya.

She couldn't speak.

Then Rebecca said something that made her blood run cold.

“The child remembers what happened in Room Seven. She remembers the woman who died.”

The recording crackled.

“I don't know whether the doctors can permanently suppress that memory. But I know they are afraid of what she'll remember if she ever sees the original footage.”

A loud noise sounded in the background.

Rebecca gasped.

Someone had entered the room.

A man's voice spoke.

“Turn that off.”

The recording ended abruptly.

Maya sat motionless.

Room Seven.

The same room number written on the back of the photograph.

“The woman who died,” she whispered.

Daniel removed the cassette.

“We need to find that footage.”

Maya looked at the clock.

3:41 p.m.

Her phone vibrated.

Unknown number.

You are getting closer.

Another message arrived.

At 4:00 p.m., you will see a dead woman.

Maya looked at Daniel.

“It's starting again.”

He took the phone and read the message.

“We should leave the hotel.”

“Why?”

“Because every time you get close to something, they know.”

Maya stood.

“Then let's find the footage before they can stop us.”

They returned to Meridian House shortly before four.

The building's main entrance had been sealed with metal panels, but Daniel knew a service route through the basement. He had discovered it during his earlier investigation.

They entered through a drainage passage and climbed a narrow staircase.

The air grew colder as they descended.

At the bottom, they found a corridor lined with old storage rooms.

One door had the number seven painted above it.

Maya stopped.

She could hear something.

A child crying.

She pressed her hands against her ears.

The sound grew louder.

A woman shouted.

A door slammed.

Then a voice whispered:

“You must never tell anyone what you saw.”

Maya staggered backward.

Daniel caught her.

“Maya? What's happening?”

She stared at the door.

“I've been here before.”

He helped her stand.

“Are you sure?”

She nodded.

“I remember the smell. The lights. There was a red chair in the corner.”

Daniel looked through the small window in the door.

The room was empty.

Except for a metal chair in the corner.

It was red.

Maya pushed past him and opened the door.

The memories came rushing back.

She was seven years old.

She was sitting on the red chair, holding a stuffed rabbit.

Her mother stood beside her, crying.

Rebecca knelt in front of her.

“Listen to me, Maya,” Rebecca whispered. “Whatever happens, you must remember that your mother loves you.”

The child nodded.

Then Dr. Shaw entered the room.

He carried a folder.

Behind him stood Maya's father.

Samuel Cole.

“It's time,” Shaw said.

Maya's mother grabbed her daughter's hand.

“No. We agreed she would leave.”

Samuel looked away.

“I changed my mind.”

Evelyn stared at him in disbelief.

“You promised me!”

“I have no choice.”

“There is always a choice!”

Shaw moved toward the child.

Rebecca stood between them.

“Don't touch her.”

The room erupted into shouting.

Maya remembered her father grabbing her mother.

She remembered Rebecca pushing Shaw away.

She remembered a sharp sound.

A scream.

Then blood.

Maya collapsed to her knees.

Daniel knelt beside her.

“Maya!”

She couldn't hear him.

The memory continued.

Rebecca lay on the floor.

A knife was beside her hand.

The little girl stood over her, crying.

Her white dress was covered in blood.

Then Samuel Cole crouched in front of his daughter.

He took her face in his hands.

“Look at me, Maya.”

She sobbed.

“Daddy, I didn't mean to.”

He held her tighter.

“You didn't do anything wrong.”

“But she's dead.”

“No, sweetheart. She isn't dead.”

He looked toward Dr. Shaw.

“Prepare the procedure.”

Maya gasped.

The room around her seemed to dissolve.

She could hear Daniel calling her name, but she was back in the past, watching her father carry her out of Room Seven.

Behind them, Rebecca lay motionless on the floor.

Her eyes were open.

And she was looking directly at Maya.

---

## The Dead Woman

Maya woke on the floor of Room Seven.

Daniel knelt beside her, his face pale with fear.

“How long was I unconscious?” she asked.

“About two minutes.”

She sat up slowly.

“I remember.”

“Remember what?”

“Rebecca.”

Daniel's expression changed.

“What happened?”

Maya looked at the red chair.

“I saw her die.”

He went very still.

“Are you sure?”

“I was there. I saw everything.”

She told him about the argument, the knife, and her father's decision to take her away.

Daniel listened without interrupting.

When she finished, he looked as though someone had struck him.

“My sister was murdered,” he whispered.

Maya nodded.

“But I don't think I killed her.”

“Why?”

“Because I remember her reaching for me. I remember her trying to protect me. I remember my father telling me she wasn't dead.”

Daniel looked down.

“What if he was lying?”

Maya shook her head.

“No. I think he was trying to make me believe she was dead.”

“Why would he do that?”

“Because if I believed she was alive, I'd keep looking for her.”

Daniel stood and walked to the doorway.

For several seconds, he stared into the corridor.

Then he turned back.

“We need to find the original archive.”

They searched the storage rooms until they found a staircase hidden behind a metal cabinet. It led to a narrow chamber beneath the building.

The walls were lined with shelves.

Hundreds of folders sat in orderly rows, each marked with a number.

Maya found Subject 014.

Inside were photographs, medical notes, and several recordings.

One document contained a handwritten entry from her father.

SUBJECT EXHIBITS PERSISTENT RECALL OF THE ROOM SEVEN INCIDENT. RECOMMEND DISCONTINUATION OF STANDARD MEMORY SUPPRESSION PROTOCOL.

Another note was dated three days later.

SUBJECT HAS BEEN INFORMED THAT REBECCA OKAFOR DIED DURING AN ACCIDENTAL ALTERCATION. SUBJECT SHOWS SIGNS OF DISTRESS BUT CANNOT RELIABLY RECALL THE EVENT.

Maya's hands trembled.

She turned the page.

MOTHER HAS BEEN REMOVED FROM THE FACILITY. FATHER REMAINS COOPERATIVE.

The next page contained a photograph of Evelyn.

She was sitting in a room with no windows, her face bruised.

Beneath the photograph was a note.

EVELYN COLE REFUSES TO DISCLOSE THE LOCATION OF THE ORIGINAL RECORDING.

Maya closed the folder.

Her mother hadn't abandoned her.

She had been imprisoned.

For eleven years.

Maya felt a wave of grief so intense that she could barely breathe.

Daniel placed a hand on her shoulder.

“We'll find her.”

She nodded.

Then she noticed a small black box on the bottom shelf.

It had no label, only a number engraved on the lid.

015.

She opened it.

Inside was a photograph of a young woman.

The woman looked exactly like Rebecca.

But she was older than in the other photographs.

Her hair was shorter, and a thin scar crossed her chin.

Maya turned the picture over.

A date had been written on the back.

Three months ago.

Beneath it were five words.

SUBJECT 015 — STATUS: ACTIVE.

Maya stared at the photograph.

“Daniel.”

He took it from her.

His face went white.

“That's impossible.”

“Why?”

“Because Subject 015 was recorded as deceased.”

Maya looked at the folder again.

The final page contained a single sentence.

SUBJECT 015 HAS BEEN TRANSFERRED TO THE LAZARUS RECOVERY PROGRAM.

Daniel's hands began to shake.

“Rebecca is alive.”

Before Maya could answer, footsteps sounded above them.

Someone had entered the building.

A door slammed.

Then a man's voice echoed through the corridor.

“Miss Cole?”

Dr. Shaw.

“We know you're down there.”

Daniel grabbed the folder and pulled Maya toward the staircase.

They hurried through the chamber, but the exit had been blocked by a heavy metal door.

Maya tried the handle.

It wouldn't move.

Daniel searched the wall for another way out.

Behind them, footsteps approached.

Shaw's voice grew closer.

“You don't understand what you're doing, Maya. Your father spent years trying to protect you from these memories.”

“You murdered Rebecca!” Maya shouted.

A pause.

Then Shaw laughed softly.

“Is that what you remember?”

Maya froze.

Shaw continued.

“Memory is not a recording. It changes every time you recall it. It is influenced by fear, expectation, and suggestion.”

“You're lying.”

“Perhaps. But ask yourself something.”

His footsteps stopped outside the chamber.

“If Rebecca was dead, why did your father keep paying for her treatment?”

Daniel stared at Maya.

The question hung in the air.

Shaw spoke again.

“Your father never stopped trying to save her. And neither did I.”

A lock clicked.

The metal door began to open.

Daniel grabbed Maya's hand.

“Run!”

They slipped through a narrow gap behind the shelves and entered a maintenance tunnel. The tunnel emerged outside the building, near the old chapel.

They didn't stop until they reached the car.

Maya looked at the photograph of Rebecca.

Alive.

Somewhere.

The woman she had seen lying on the floor eleven years ago might never have died.

Perhaps her father had staged the incident.

Perhaps Shaw had manipulated the records.

Or perhaps Rebecca had survived something that should have killed her.

Maya's phone vibrated.

A new message appeared.

DAY THREE IS OVER.

Another followed.

TOMORROW, YOU WILL MEET THE DEAD WOMAN.

Maya stared at the screen.

Then her phone rang.

Unknown number.

She answered.

A woman's voice whispered, “Maya?”

She recognized it immediately.

Rebecca.

“Who is this?” Maya asked, although she already knew.

“I'm the woman you killed.”

Maya's eyes filled with tears.

“Are you alive?”

A long silence followed.

Then Rebecca spoke.

“I don't know anymore.”

The call ended.

Maya lowered the phone.

Daniel stared at her.

“What did she say?”

Maya looked at the photograph.

“She said she's the woman I killed.”

Daniel stepped back.

“That doesn't make sense.”

“No,” Maya whispered. “It doesn't.”

Her phone vibrated one last time.

A photograph appeared on the screen.

It showed Rebecca standing in a dark room, facing a mirror.

Behind her stood a second woman.

Maya's mother.

Both women were looking directly at the camera.

Beneath the photograph was a message.

TOMORROW AT MIDNIGHT, ONE OF THEM WILL DIE.

Maya looked at Daniel.

“Which one?”

He shook his head.

“I don't know.”

Then another message arrived.

CHOOSE CAREFULLY, MAYA.

**END OF EPISODE 3**

**NEXT EPISODE: EPISODE 4 — SOMEONE INSIDE**
